# Introduction

Bray-Curtis and its relatives compare metaproteomes by accession: two
different proteins count as unrelated even when they share fold and function.
`repdist` compares them in the representation space of a protein language
model, by default TM-Vec, where the cosine similarity of two proteins is their
predicted TM-score. This vignette covers its beta-diversity side:

- **Compare samples.** `sample_mmd()` gives a sample-by-sample distance, the
    maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), for PERMANOVA and ordination.

Protein-level clustering and differential abundance
(`protein_similarity()`, `bin_proteins()`, `bin_glom()`) have their own
[clustering vignette](clustering.html), `vignette("clustering")`.

This vignette runs the workflow on simulated data with a known answer; the
[inputs](#inputs) section shows the files you would start from instead. The
[simulation page](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/simulation.html)
benchmarks it over many such contrasts, and the
[case study](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/case_study.html) applies it to
a real metaproteome.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
# dependencies = TRUE also installs vegan and ggplot2, used below
BiocManager::install("repdist", dependencies = TRUE)
```

```{r libs}
library(repdist)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Data

## The experiment

Picture two groups of ten microbial community metaproteomes. Every sample
holds the same thousand-odd background enzymes at similar abundances; the
groups differ in one extra function. Each sample of group A carries a little
more nucleotidyltransferase activity (EC 2.7.7), each sample of group B a
little more aminoacyltransferase activity (EC 2.3.2), and every sample gets
that extra activity from different enzymes of the class, unrelated in
sequence. So the groups differ in what their proteins do, not in which
proteins they hold. A distance that compares accessions, like Bray-Curtis,
cannot see that; a distance that knows two enzymes of one class look alike
should.

`simulate_ec` builds this from 1,160 bacterial and archaeal Swiss-Prot
enzymes with experimentally supported EC numbers: every enzyme of the two
classes, plus 1,000 other enzymes as background. Every enzyme has a positive
expected abundance in all 20 samples, and in each sample 5% of the abundance
goes to two extra enzymes of its group's class, with negative-binomial counts
drawn around that. No two of these 40 enriched enzymes share a 50%-identity
sequence cluster. `?simulate_ec` and the
[data provenance](https://github.com/Yixuan39/repdist/blob/main/inst/scripts/DATA_PROVENANCE.md)
give the details.

## Inputs

`repdist` needs three inputs, each usually a file:

- **Protein sequences**: a FASTA file, one record per protein, the protein
    ID first in the header. `embed_proteins()` reads it and adds the
    embeddings; `read_embeddings()` reads embeddings the `tmvec`
    command-line tool already made.
- **Counts**: a tab-separated table, samples in rows, sample IDs in the
    first column and protein IDs as column names; PSM or spectral counts.
- **Sample metadata**: a tab-separated table, one row per sample, a
    `sample` column plus the variables to test.

`inst/extdata` ships one of each, 100 proteins of a mouse gut metaproteome
(Blakeley-Ruiz et al. 2025) in 23 samples on two diets, along with the
proteins' embeddings as the `tmvec` command-line tool writes them:

```{r files}
ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "repdist")
readLines(ex("metaproteomics.fasta"), n = 2)
read.delim(ex("metaproteomics_counts.tsv"), row.names = 1,
    check.names = FALSE)[1:3, 1:3]
head(read.delim(ex("metaproteomics_samples.tsv")), 3)
```

The rest of this vignette takes the same three inputs from `simulate_ec`.
Each step below runs on it; its commented-out lines show the same step on
files of your own.

## Protein sequences and embeddings

`sample_mmd()` compares proteins by their embeddings, one vector per protein
from the protein language model. `embed_proteins()` computes them from a
FASTA file; it does not run in this vignette, because its first call
downloads the model (up to a few GB). `simulate_ec` ships its embeddings
precomputed.

```{r proteins}
data(simulate_ec, package = "repdist")
proteins <- simulate_ec$proteins
# proteins <- embed_proteins("path/on/your/proteins.fasta")
# or, embeddings from the tmvec command-line tool:
# proteins <- read_embeddings("path/on/your/db.npz",
#     "path/on/your/proteins.fasta")
proteins
dim(S4Vectors::mcols(proteins)$embedding)
```

`proteins` is an `AAStringSet` of the sequences. `names(proteins)` are the
protein IDs, which must match the count table's column names, and
`mcols(proteins)$embedding` is the embedding matrix, one unit-norm row per
protein.

## Counts

```{r counts}
counts <- simulate_ec$counts
# counts <- as.matrix(read.delim("path/on/your/counts.tsv", row.names = 1,
#     check.names = FALSE))
counts[1:3, 1:4]
```

`counts` is a samples-by-proteins matrix of PSM-like counts.

## Sample metadata

```{r samples}
samples <- simulate_ec$samples
# samples <- read.delim("path/on/your/samples.tsv")
head(samples, 3)
```

`samples` has one row per sample, in the order of `rownames(counts)`. `group`
is what the test below compares; `enriched_ec3` is the class the sample was
enriched for.

## Annotation

```{r annotation}
annotation <- simulate_ec$annotation
head(annotation[, c("protein", "ec3", "mmseqs30", "enriched_in")], 3)
```

`annotation` has one row per protein: its name, organism and length, EC
labels (`ec3`, `ec4`), MMseqs2 sequence clusters at 50% and 30% identity
(`mmseqs50`, `mmseqs30`), and `enriched_in`, the sample an enriched enzyme
was added to (`NA` for background). It is the simulation's ground truth:
below, only the Bray-Curtis baseline reads it, for `mmseqs30`. `repdist`
itself never needs an annotation.

# Relative abundance

`sample_mmd()` and Bray-Curtis both compare relative abundances. Bray-Curtis
also gets a sequence-cluster version: counts summed within MMseqs2 clusters
at 30% identity (`annotation$mmseqs30`), its analogue of a repdist protein
bin.

```{r relabund}
relative <- counts / rowSums(counts)
mmseqs30 <- t(rowsum(t(relative), annotation[colnames(relative), "mmseqs30"]))
```

# Distance

`sample_mmd()` compares the samples' abundance-weighted distributions over
the embeddings.

```{r distance}
D <- list(
    MMD = sample_mmd(relative, proteins),
    `Bray-Curtis, MMseqs2 30%` = vegdist(mmseqs30, "bray"),
    `Bray-Curtis, protein` = vegdist(relative, "bray")
)
```

# PERMANOVA

`adonis2()` tests whether the groups differ under each distance.

```{r permanova}
perm <- t(vapply(D, function(Dk) {
    set.seed(1)
    a <- adonis2(Dk ~ group, data = samples, permutations = 999)
    c(R2 = a$R2[1], p = a$`Pr(>F)`[1])
}, numeric(2)))
round(perm, 3)
```

# PCoA

`cmdscale()` draws each distance's principal coordinates; ellipses are 95%
data ellipses per group.

```{r pcoa}
#| fig.width: 9
#| fig.height: 3.8
#| fig.alt: "PCoA of MMD and two Bray-Curtis distances, 95% group ellipses"
pcoa <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(D), function(k) {
    pc <- cmdscale(D[[k]], k = 2, eig = TRUE)
    pct <- round(100 * pc$eig[1:2] / sum(pc$eig[pc$eig > 0]))
    data.frame(samples, PCo1 = pc$points[, 1], PCo2 = pc$points[, 2],
        distance = sprintf("%s\nPCo1 %d%%, PCo2 %d%%", k, pct[1], pct[2]))
}))
pcoa$distance <- factor(pcoa$distance, unique(pcoa$distance))
ggplot(pcoa, aes(PCo1, PCo2, colour = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    stat_ellipse(level = 0.95) + # 95% data ellipse per group
    facet_wrap(~distance, scales = "free") +
    theme_bw()
```

MMD separates the groups and Bray-Curtis does not, on proteins or on sequence
clusters: no enriched protein is shared, and the 40 enriched enzymes fall in 37
different 30% clusters, so to Bray-Curtis every enrichment looks like noise.
MMD credits enzymes of one class for being close in the embedding space.

# Notes

`sample_mmd()` holds a protein-by-protein kernel matrix, so on real data use
the proteins identified in your samples, never a whole search database:
20,000 proteins take about 3 GB. The
[clustering vignette](clustering.html) covers protein-level clustering and
differential abundance, built on the same embeddings.
